6.1 — Gravity & Jump: The First Flick

The cave is the first place in this game where down means something. Walk off the edge of the floor and you do not fall — you keep walking, level. Today you turn gravity back on for one scene, and use the same body to throw the character into the air with J.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I jump?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

The character falls, and then it jumps. "Make the player jump" is really two mechanisms wearing one name: a world that pulls you down, and one instant where the body is handed an upward velocity that the pulling-down then spends. Neither half exists in the cave today, and the same prefab must keep NOT falling in the world you built it for.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the Player a body that falls in this sceneBody Type Dynamic and Gravity Scale above zero - it takes both. Gravity Scale multiplies the project gravity Physics 2D has at -9.81 on Y. Your body has been Dynamic with Gravity Scale 0 since 2.1.Read: the rb.gravityScale row of the quick reference.
  2. Ask the scene what it is calledThe same prefab is played in both worlds, so "am I in the cave?" is a fact about the scene, not about the prefab: SceneManager.GetActiveScene().name compared against the one name that means top-down.Read: the SceneManager row in the quick reference.
  3. Turn gravity on once, when the scene loadsA gated write in Start(): read the name once, then hand the body a gravity scale. Once, before the first frame - in Update() the same number is written sixty times a second.Read: the void Start() row of the quick reference.
  4. Notice one press of the jump keyInput.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) inside the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4. True on the single frame the key goes down; GetKey is true on every frame it is held - a jump is a moment, not a state.Read: the Input.GetKeyDown(...) row of the quick reference.
  5. Hand the body one upward flick, and let gravity spend itrb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse): one instant change in momentum on the Y axis only. The height is the impulse divided by mass, the rise is paid for by the gravity from part 1, and the apex is the frame the vertical velocity reaches zero.Read: the rb.AddForceY(...) row of the quick reference.

Three of those five parts are work you have already done: a Dynamic body is 2.1, a key check is 1.4 and 5.2, and a once-only write in Start() is 3.3. The other two have no precedent, which is why this lesson walks every line.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the player jump" cannot be looked up - there is no such API. "Push a rigidbody upward once" can.

Your turn

The name check in part 2 is the first thing you have ever asked the engine about the world rather than about the player. Name one other fact about the scene in your game, and say where you would keep it.

Part 4 notices a key press; part 5 moves the body. Nothing in the file measures time, and yet the arc has a height. Where does the height come from - and which part would you change first if the jump felt wrong?

In the Editor ~20 min
  1. Project window → open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity — the cave — then Game view → press Play and walk off the edge of the floor. Nothing falls, and that is not a bug: the Rigidbody2D you gave the Player in 2.1 has Gravity Scale 0, because a top-down character who obeys gravity falls through the world forever. You were right then. The cave is the first place where you are wrong.
  2. Hierarchy → select the Player, then Inspector → Rigidbody2D → Gravity Scale. Set it to 1 while the game is running and watch the character drop. Then try 0.2 and describe the difference out loud.
  3. Game view → stop Play, then Inspector → Gravity Scale: it is back to 0. Inspector edits made during Play are thrown away on Stop (1.2) — which is why the cave's gravity has to end up in code.
  4. Hierarchy → open the Overworld scene — the top-down hub — select its Player, and set Inspector → Gravity Scale to 1. Game view → press Play: you have just broken the hub. Write down what it cost, then set it back to 0.
  5. Hierarchy → put the two Players side by side in your head. Both are blue prefab instances of the same Player. One must fall, one must not. Before you read the walkthrough, write down the one place you would put that difference — the script, the prefab, or the scene — and one reason for it.
In the Code ~30 min

Two lookups and two decisions: what the Rigidbody2D offers, and the four ways a body can leave the ground.

Field on the Rigidbody2DWhat it actually does
Body Type Dynamic bodies fall and are pushed. Kinematic bodies move only where code puts them, and ignore gravity, forces and mass entirely — if your character stands still in mid-air with Gravity Scale 5, look here first.
Gravity Scale A multiplier on the project-wide gravity (Project Settings, Physics 2D, Y at -9.81). 0 is off, 1 is undiluted. Means nothing on a Kinematic body.
Mass How much the same force moves you. Gravity pulls harder on a heavy body, so mass cancels out in a fall — but a force you apply by hand divides by mass.
Constraints Freeze Rotation Z, set in 2.2 so the character stops tumbling. It matters in the air too: an unfrozen body spins when it clips a corner mid-jump.
TechniqueWhat it requiresWhat it costs
rb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse) A Dynamic body and Gravity Scale above 0. Mass divides into it, so retuning mass silently retunes every jump. Clean parabola — the row the walkthrough builds.
rb.linearVelocityY = jumpSpeed A Dynamic body and Gravity Scale above 0. Identical height every time, to the pixel — and it erases whatever vertical motion was already there: a platform's lift, a knockback, a bounce.
AddForceY(thrust, ForceMode2D.Force) every frame while held A Dynamic body; some rule that stops it — fuel, ceiling, timer. A rocket, not a jump. Height depends on how long you hold — and this is what you get by accident if you forget the force mode.
MovePosition() in steps A Kinematic body, moved in FixedUpdate(). It ignores gravity, so it never falls, and it only collides with Dynamic bodies — so no floor is solid to it, and no OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D collision) fires against those static colliders. The cave door runs on that callback and would go silent.
Architectural specification: how does your script know it is in the cave? Your movement code assumes a top-down world, and the script has to be told which world it woke up in. All four options below are used in real projects; the walkthrough builds (a).
  • (a) Ask the scene its name — SceneManager.GetActiveScene().name against "Overworld". Readable, no setup; breaks silently if someone renames the scene. This game's choice.
  • (b) Ask the scene its build index — the cave is index 2. Survives a rename; lies when the build order changes. SceneSwitch.cs already does this.
  • (c) A serialized bool, ticked per scene instance — visible in the Inspector without pressing Play. Costs a tick on every new Player somebody places, and a tick is easy to forget.
  • (d) A component that only exists on the cave's Player — the component's presence is the flag. Costs one more file and one more lookup.
  • Whatever you pick, reuse a scene-mode flag you already built this year: two flags meaning "which world am I in" is how a project starts rotting.
Architectural specification: gravity and the flick.
  • Where does the cave's gravity get turned on? Name the exact point in the lifecycle — a field default, Start(), or every frame — and say what breaks at the other two.
  • Which key, and which of GetKey or GetKeyDown? Say what holding the key for two seconds does under each.
  • Is your jump force a serialized field or a magic number? Does its name say force or speed — and what does the name make the next reader believe?
  • How do you know the jump worked? Name what you would print, and what it proves.

Socratic: Gravity Is a Number You Own

  1. Real gravity is a constant of the universe. Unity ships it as an Inspector field. Why would an engine make a law of physics editable per object?
  2. Same Player prefab, same script, two worlds: the hub needs Gravity Scale 0 and the cave needs it above 0. Where should that difference live — the script, the scene, or both?
  3. A Kinematic body ignores gravity, forces and mass entirely. Set Body Type to Kinematic in the cave, and what would your jump code have to do instead to look like a jump?
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how does my script know it is in the cave?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. The cave and the Overworld play the same prefab, so "which world am I in" cannot live on the prefab: it is a fact about the scene, and it has to reach the script before the first frame runs. One import, one field, one read, one line.

Step 1Ask the engine for the scene, and declare the field that remembers the answer

One using at the top of the file, and one plain field in the class body beside speed - no [SerializeField], because nothing in the Inspector is going to set it.

using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;
    bool isPlatformer = false;
  1. 1The namespace that holds the scene API. Without it the name SceneManager does not exist in this file, and the compiler says so in a way that looks like a typo.Imports are how C# keeps its namespaces from colliding. Every type you have used so far - MonoBehaviour, Input, Vector2 - arrived through one of the two using lines Unity writes at the top for you. This is the first one you have had to add yourself.
  2. 2Which world this Player woke up in. Private, because only this script needs it, and not serialized, because Start() is about to decide it - an Inspector box you still have to tick by hand is a fact you have to remember, not a fact the code knows.Why keep the flag at all, if Start() already knows? Because Update() runs every frame and needs the answer sixty times a second, and asking the scene engine sixty times a second to answer a question that cannot change is work for nothing. Read the world once, remember it in a bool.

Step 2Read the scene name once, and decide gravity from it

The body lookup you have had in Start() since 2.2 is unchanged. What is new is four lines underneath it.

        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();

        Scene currentScene = SceneManager.GetActiveScene();
        if (currentScene.name == "Overworld")
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 0;
        }
        else
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 1;
            isPlatformer = true;
        }
  1. 1The reference you already cache here - the body about to be given a gravity scale. It sits on the same GameObject as this script, which is why the plain lookup finds it.
  2. 3One question, asked once. GetActiveScene() hands back the scene that is loaded right now, and .name will be the string you see in the Hierarchy when the scene file was saved: "Start", "Overworld", "Platformer".Read once, in a method that runs once. Start() is the once-only setup method from 1.3, and a fact about the scene belongs there. The same call inside Update() would be a hundred and twenty string comparisons a second to answer a question whose answer never changes.
  3. 4The only world in this game that is top-down. Note which way round it reads: we name the ONE scene that does not get gravity, so a new cave scene is platformer by default - the safe way to be wrong.This is the fragile line in the lesson, and you should know it is fragile. Spell the scene name wrong - a typo, or somebody renames the scene file - and the comparison is simply false, the character gets gravity anyway, and nothing errors. No compiler catches a wrong string. Type it, then look at the Hierarchy to confirm it matches.
  4. 6The hub stays on the floor. rb.gravityScale is the Rigidbody2D property behind the Inspector field you have been reading all year, and 0 means "ignore the project gravity".
  5. 8Every other scene falls. Start and the cave both take this branch, which is why the Player in Start.unity had better be standing on something.Why an else rather than two ifs? Because a body of gravity scale 0 or 1 with no third state is the whole decision. One branch that always runs is one fewer thing to get wrong.
  6. 10The whole of turning gravity on. 1 means "the project gravity, undiluted" - Project Settings, Physics 2D, Y at -9.81.Why this is code and not a number in the Inspector. You could set the cave copy to 1 by hand and write nothing - but that number is invisible to a reader of your script, and has to be repeated on every new Player anyone places.
  7. 11Record the answer. This is the flag Update() will ask about: it decides which movement model runs, and later it decides whether a jump key is even listened for.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. Two things are worth naming. First, the flag buys you nothing today - Start() could have set gravity and left it at that. It earns its keep in the next step, when Update() has to choose between two movement models, and again in 6.2 when the jump key only exists in the cave. Writing the flag before you need it is cheaper than threading it through afterwards.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;

// PlayerController.cs - the gravity half, complete. Everything from 1.4 to 5.3
// (input, movement, animation, coins, health) stays exactly as you wrote it;
// the import, the flag and the four lines under the body lookup are the whole
// of what is new.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 4;              // your number from 2.2
    bool isPlatformer = false;    // which world did I wake up in?

    Rigidbody2D rb;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();               // looked up once, per 2.2

        // Asked once, for both worlds. The Overworld keeps 0 because this line
        // says so, not because nobody wrote anything - the decision is visible
        // to anyone reading this file instead of only to the Inspector.
        Scene currentScene = SceneManager.GetActiveScene();
        if (currentScene.name == "Overworld")
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 0;
            isPlatformer = false;
        }
        else
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 1;
            isPlatformer = true;
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... the input, movement and animation lines from 1.4, 1.6, 2.2 and 5.3 ...
    }
}
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I make the character leave the ground?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. There is no Jump() in Unity, and nobody is going to give you one. The gravity half is already in your file, so what is left is a number to tune, a key check, one push, and a way to see that it worked. The push is where every mistake in this lesson happens.

Step 1Declare how hard the flick is

One field, in the class body next to speed - and serialized, unlike the flag: it is a number a designer tunes, and a designer should not have to open a code editor to tune it.

    [SerializeField] float jumpForce;
  1. 1How hard the flick is. Serialized, so it appears in the Inspector under Player Controller and can be changed without touching this file - which is what a tuning number is for.No starting value, and that is deliberate. A field with no initializer is whatever the Inspector says, and the cave's Player already carries 10 for this name. Write = 7f and you have written a number that the Inspector silently overwrites, which is the most confusing kind of default there is. Fill it in the Inspector instead.

Step 2Notice the press, once, at the bottom of Update()

Four lines at the end of the Update() you have been adding to since 1.4 - after your movement and animation lines, beside the key check you wrote for the lever in 5.2.

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && isPlatformer)
        {
            Jump();
        }
  1. 1Input is the class from 1.4, KeyCode.J names the key, GetKeyDown is true on the single frame the key goes down, and isPlatformer is the flag from the gravity half doing its second job.Input.GetKey(KeyCode.J) here is the wrong one, and it fails in the loudest way there is. Without the Down it is true on every frame the key is held, so half a second of holding J applies thirty pushes and the character leaves the top of the level. The jump looks broken; the condition is. And the check belongs in Update(): FixedUpdate() is the physics clock, which can run several times in one frame or skip frames, so a one-frame press can be counted twice or missed.
  2. 3A call, not the push itself. The next line puts the push in a method with a name - the shape 5.2 taught you to reach for, and the shape this course keeps asking for: when a line is about to grow, give it a name first.

Step 3Write the push, and say why it is one instant

A new method below Update(), beside your others.

    void Jump()
    {
        rb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
    print("jump");
  1. 1Not private, not public - in C#, a method with no modifier is private by default, the same as the fields. Unity calls nothing here; only your own Update() does.
  2. 3The flick. AddForceY is the Y-axis shorthand for "add this much force upward" - the same call as AddForce(new Vector2(0, jumpForce), ForceMode2D.Impulse), with the zero written for you.The second argument is the whole lesson, and leaving it out is the classic bug. With ForceMode2D.Impulse this is one hit, spent at the next physics step. Without it the default is a force that keeps applying while the calls keep coming - and since this line sits inside a check true on exactly one frame, you get a dribble so small the character twitches and settles. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and "my jump does nothing" is what you write in the group chat.
  3. 5One line, inside Jump(), that proves the key check fired. Unity's print is Debug.Log() with a shorter name, and it is the only instrument this lesson gives you: if the Console says jump and the character does not move, the problem is the physics or the gravity, not the input.Delete it before you move on. An instrument, not a feature. A print left here fills the Console with a line per press and buries the next real error under them.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

This is not the end of the story, and the Console will tell you so within a minute of playing: hold J against nothing and the character climbs, because nothing here counts how many jumps you have left. That is not a mistake to fix today. Play with it until you can describe exactly what is wrong, then bring that description to 6.2.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;

// PlayerController.cs - gravity for the cave, and one flick upward.
// The gravity half came first; the jump assumes it. Up, apex, down: the
// only line that makes the arc is the force, and gravity does the rest.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 4;              // your number from 2.2
    bool isPlatformer = false;    // which world did I wake up in?

    Rigidbody2D rb;

    [SerializeField] float jumpForce;   // how hard the flick is - set in the Inspector

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();   // looked up once, never inside Update()

        Scene currentScene = SceneManager.GetActiveScene();
        if (currentScene.name == "Overworld")
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 0;
            isPlatformer = false;
        }
        else
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 1;
            isPlatformer = true;
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... input, movement and animation, from 1.4 to 5.3 ...

        if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && isPlatformer)
        {
            Jump();
        }
    }

    // The whole jump. One impulse, and gravity spends it over the next half
    // second - which is why there is nothing here about coming back down.
    void Jump()
    {
        print("jump");
        rb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
}
Build Lab: Tune It ~20 min

Change one number at a time and write one sentence of feel for each, in a file you keep. Three knobs, and the third one is the interesting one.

KnobTry
jumpForce — Inspector → Player Controllerhalf, then double
Gravity Scale — Inspector → Rigidbody2D0.2, then 1, then 4
Mass — Inspector → Rigidbody2D1, then 5 — watch the jump and the fall
Gravity off plus an impulse is not a jump — it is an escape. Leave the cave's Player at Gravity Scale 0 and add an impulse and the character rises and never stops rising. No error, no warning, no ceiling. When a jump "works but feels wrong", read Gravity Scale and Body Type before you touch your code.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain Gravity Scale, Body Type and Mass as three separate ideas, not one
  • Say where the cave's gravity gets turned on, and prove the top-down world still works
  • Compare the four ways to leave the ground and defend the one you wrote
  • Explain Force versus Impulse in feel-words, and the parabola gravity spends
  • Commit and push
